questions.text: Explain how I2C works and when you would choose it over SPI.

concepts.text: Two wires: SDA and SCL, shared synchronous bus
Devices are addressed, supports multiple slaves with unique addresses
Open-drain lines require pull-up resistors
Slower transfer speed than SPI but requires fewer microcontroller pins

questions.idealAnswer: I2C is a synchronous, half-duplex serial protocol using two open-drain bidirectional lines: SDA and SCL, both requiring pull-up resistors. Each slave device has a unique address. You would choose I2C over SPI when conserving pins is important or when connecting many peripherals, though SPI is faster and full-duplex.

questions.text: Explain how the SPI communication bus works and how slave devices are selected.

concepts.text: Uses MOSI, MISO, SCK/SCLK, and Chip Select / Slave Select lines
Dedicated active-low Chip Select line for each peripheral
Full-duplex synchronous data transmission with separate data lines

questions.idealAnswer: SPI is a four-wire synchronous serial protocol with MOSI, MISO, SCLK, and individual Chip Select (CS) lines for each slave. Data is shifted simultaneously in full duplex. A slave is selected by pulling its dedicated CS line low.

questions.text: How does asynchronous serial communication (UART) work without a shared clock signal?

concepts.text: Both devices must be pre-configured with the exact same baud rate
Frames use start and stop bits (and optional parity) to synchronize byte boundaries
Asynchronous point-to-point communication over TX and RX wires

questions.idealAnswer: UART is asynchronous; there is no shared clock. Both devices agree in advance on a baud rate. Synchronization happens on the falling edge of a start bit for every byte frame, followed by data bits, optional parity, and stop bits.

questions.text: What is Direct Memory Access (DMA), and why is it essential in high-throughput embedded systems?

concepts.text: Transfers data between peripherals and memory without CPU intervention
Hardware controller manages memory bus addressing and burst transfers
Frees CPU cycles and drastically reduces interrupt overhead at high data rates

questions.idealAnswer: DMA is a hardware feature allowing peripherals to transfer blocks of data directly to/from memory without CPU involvement. It prevents CPU starvation from frequent interrupts during high-throughput tasks like audio buffering or ADC streaming.

questions.text: Explain the difference between polling and interrupts, and how an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) should be designed.

concepts.text: Polling wastes CPU cycles in loops whereas interrupts provide immediate event-driven response
ISRs must be kept as short and fast as possible without blocking calls or delays
Hardware saves CPU registers on the stack and switches execution context

questions.idealAnswer: Polling repeatedly checks a status flag in a loop, wasting CPU cycles, while interrupts notify the CPU immediately when an event occurs. An ISR should be minimal: acknowledge the hardware flag, copy essential data or set a notification flag, and exit quickly without delays or blocking.

questions.text: How do hardware timers and Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) work in a microcontroller?

concepts.text: Clock prescaler divides system frequency to drive a counter register
PWM duty cycle represents the fraction of time the signal remains high over a period
Output compare registers toggle pin state when counter matches value

questions.idealAnswer: A hardware timer uses a prescaler to divide the core clock and increments a counter. In PWM mode, an output compare register compares against the counter: the pin stays high until the match, then drops low until period reset, generating a variable duty cycle signal.

questions.text: What is the difference between push-pull, open-drain, and pull-up/pull-down configurations on GPIO pins?

concepts.text: Push-pull actively drives both high (VCC) and low (GND) with complementary transistors
Open-drain only pulls to ground, relying on external pull-up for high level
Internal pull-up/down resistors prevent floating inputs from picking up electrical noise

questions.idealAnswer: Push-pull drives both high and low rails using paired transistors. Open-drain can only sink current to ground, requiring an external pull-up to pull high. Internal pull-up or pull-down resistors prevent floating high-impedance inputs from oscillating due to noise.

questions.text: What causes switch contact bounce, and how can you debounce a digital input in firmware?

concepts.text: Mechanical switch contacts physically oscillate rapidly before settling
Software debouncing checks state stability over time using timers or state machines
Prevents false multiple triggers or interrupts on a single press

questions.idealAnswer: Mechanical spring contacts bounce upon closing, generating false rapid transitions. Software debouncing samples the input periodically with a timer and confirms the state remains stable for 10-50 milliseconds before declaring a valid press.

questions.text: In C, why and when must you use the 'volatile' keyword in embedded systems programming?

concepts.text: Tells compiler not to optimize away or cache memory reads in CPU registers
Required for memory-mapped I/O hardware peripheral registers
Required for variables modified asynchronously inside an ISR or another thread

questions.idealAnswer: The volatile qualifier tells the compiler that a variable's value can change unexpectedly outside of the current program flow. It prevents the optimizer from caching the value in a register. It is mandatory for memory-mapped peripheral registers and variables shared between main code and ISRs.

questions.text: In an RTOS, what is the fundamental difference between a mutex and a binary semaphore?

concepts.text: A mutex has an ownership concept: only the task that locked it may unlock it
A semaphore is a signaling mechanism: one task or ISR signals, another waits
Mutexes often support priority inheritance to mitigate priority inversion

questions.idealAnswer: A mutex provides mutual exclusion with ownership: the task that locks it must unlock it, and it can implement priority inheritance. A binary semaphore is a signaling flag: an ISR or task can signal (give) it, and a different task can wait (take) it, with no concept of ownership.

questions.text: What is priority inversion in an RTOS, and how does priority inheritance solve it?

concepts.text: A medium priority task preempts a low task holding a lock needed by a high task
Temporarily elevates the low priority task to the high task's priority while holding the lock
Deadlock avoidance requires strict lock ordering and timeout guards

questions.idealAnswer: Priority inversion happens when a low-priority task holds a shared resource needed by a high-priority task, but a medium-priority task preempts the low one, indefinitely delaying the high task. Priority inheritance solves this by temporarily raising the low task to the high priority until it unlocks the resource.

questions.text: Explain the memory segments in an embedded C program: Flash, RAM, Text, Data, BSS, Stack, and Heap.

concepts.text: BSS stores uninitialized or zero-initialized globals in RAM, cleared at boot
Stack grows for local variables/frames while heap is for dynamic allocations
Flash/ROM holds executable code (Text segment) and initial values of Data segment

questions.idealAnswer: Flash holds the Text (executable instructions) and const data. RAM holds Data (initialized globals copied from Flash at startup), BSS (zero-initialized globals cleared at startup), the Stack (local function variables and return addresses), and Heap (dynamic memory).

questions.text: How do pointer arithmetic and function pointers work in embedded C hardware abstraction layers?

concepts.text: Pointer arithmetic scales offsets by the byte size of the underlying data type
Function pointers enable callback tables and polymorphic device driver interfaces
Memory-mapped register access requires strict alignment and type casting

questions.idealAnswer: Pointer arithmetic scales increments by sizeof(type), so advancing a uint32_t pointer by 1 increments the address by 4 bytes. Function pointers store addresses of executable code and are used to construct driver dispatch tables and asynchronous callback hooks.

questions.text: How do you set, clear, and toggle specific bits in a 32-bit hardware register in C?

concepts.text: Setting bits uses bitwise OR (|) with a shifted mask
Clearing bits uses bitwise AND (&) with inverted mask (~)
Toggling bits uses bitwise XOR (^)

questions.idealAnswer: To set bit n, use `REG |= (1U << n);`. To clear bit n, use `REG &= ~(1U << n);`. To toggle bit n, use `REG ^= (1U << n);`. To test bit n, evaluate `(REG & (1U << n)) != 0`.

questions.text: How does an Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) work, and what do resolution and sampling rate mean?

concepts.text: Resolution in bits defines the number of discrete digital quantization steps
Sampling rate must be at least twice the highest signal frequency to prevent aliasing (Nyquist theorem)
A stable voltage reference (VREF) is essential for measurement accuracy

questions.idealAnswer: An ADC converts continuous analog voltage into discrete digital values (e.g., a 12-bit ADC has 4096 steps relative to VREF). The Nyquist criterion requires sampling at at least twice the maximum signal frequency to prevent aliasing distortion.

questions.text: What is a Watchdog Timer (WDT) in a microcontroller, and how is it safely serviced by firmware?

concepts.text: Hardware countdown timer that resets the system if firmware hangs or deadlocks
Firmware must periodically refresh/kick it only when all critical tasks have completed
Never service the watchdog in an ISR timer interrupt, as ISRs can keep running even if main tasks hang

questions.idealAnswer: A watchdog timer is an independent hardware counter that triggers a microcontroller reset if it expires. Firmware must periodically refresh ('kick') it in the main loop after verifying healthy execution of all threads. It must never be kicked in an ISR, because interrupts can continue firing while threads are deadlocked.
